title.text: Surprise, entropy and cross-entropy measure how well a model predicts what really happens

objects.text: How does a language model turn raw scores into a probability for every next word, and how do we score it?

Mathematics for AI and Machine Learning  |  Session 17 of 18  |  Probability and statistics
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to Session 17. Last time we saw that training a model is maximum likelihood, and that the loss for classification is cross-entropy. Today we look at cross-entropy from the side of information. We ask how surprising an outcome is, how uncertain a distribution is, and how far a model is from reality.

We also see how temperature and top-p reshape a model's choices, and meet perplexity, the score you will see in every language model paper.

slides.notes:
By the end of today you can do three things. First, compute surprise, entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence by hand, and show that cross-entropy equals entropy plus KL. Second, take the softmax of Session 12, reshape it with temperature and trim it with top-p, and derive with numbers that the gradient of softmax with cross-entropy is the prediction minus the target, for a sigmoid too.

Third, compute the cross-entropy and the perplexity of a toy language model on a six word sentence. The numbers are illustrative, and the arithmetic is the same as in real training.

objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Ideas first. Then the lab, in Python or a spreadsheet. Then AI.

slides.notes:
Today has the usual shape. Ten minutes of recall from Session 16 and the question of the day. Thirty-five minutes of concepts, each with a picture and a hand example. A ten minute break. Then forty-five minutes of lab, where you compute entropy, cross-entropy, a temperature and top-p cut, a gradient and a perplexity yourself.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What does maximum likelihood estimation choose?
2.  Why do we work with the log-likelihood?
3.  Which assumption about the target gives cross-entropy as the loss?

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 16. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What does maximum likelihood estimation choose? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. The parameter value that makes the observed data most probable, which means the largest likelihood.

Question two. Why do we work with the log-likelihood? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. A product of many small probabilities underflows to zero. A sum of logarithms is stable, and the maximum stays at the same parameter.

Question three. Which assumption about the target gives cross-entropy as the loss? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. A Bernoulli assumption for yes or no, or a categorical assumption for one of many classes. Gaussian noise gives squared error.

If an answer was missing, do not worry. Your notes from last class have it. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Session 16

rows.text: What does maximum likelihood estimation choose?
The parameter value that makes the observed data most probable, which means the largest likelihood.
Why do we work with the log-likelihood?
A product of many small probabilities underflows to zero. A sum of logarithms is stable, and the maximum stays at the same parameter.
Which assumption about the target gives cross-entropy as the loss?
A Bernoulli assumption for yes or no, or a categorical assumption for one of many classes. Gaussian noise gives squared error.

objects.text: Today the Bernoulli and categorical losses get a second meaning, measured in bits as well as nats.

slides.notes: Maximum likelihood estimation chooses the parameter that makes the observed data most probable. We use the logarithm because a product of many small probabilities underflows, and a sum of logs does not. A Bernoulli or categorical assumption gives cross-entropy, while Gaussian noise gives squared error. Today we ask what cross-entropy means in terms of information, and why the same loss can be quoted in bits or in nats.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Entropy. The average surprise of a distribution, in bits with log2 or nats with ln. How uncertain the outcome is.

Cross-entropy. The average surprise when reality follows P but the model believes Q. The training loss for classification and language models.

KL divergence. Kullback-Leibler divergence: cross-entropy minus entropy. The extra cost of believing Q instead of P.

Temperature and top-p. Sampling settings. Temperature divides the logits before the softmax. Top-p keeps only the most likely words.

Perplexity. e to the power of the mean negative log-probability. The effective number of equally likely choices the model has at each word.

title.text:
Surprise: a rare event carries more
information than a common one

objects.alt: Surprise: a rare event carries more information than a common one

objects.text: The surprise (self-information) of an event with probability p is -log2(p) bits.

runs.text: A bit is the answer to one yes or no question.
Every time the probability is cut in half, the surprise grows by one bit.

slides.notes:
Start with surprise. If I tell you a fair coin showed heads, you learn little, because it was a coin flip. The bar is one bit. If I tell you a random letter from A to H was a particular one, that is one in eight, three bits.

If I tell you which of one thousand and twenty four tickets won, that is ten bits. A bit is the answer to one yes or no question, and you would need ten of them to find the winning ticket. Rare events carry more information. What would the surprise be for an event that is certain?

title.text:
Surprise is the negative
logarithm of the probability

objects.alt: Surprise is the negative logarithm of the probability

rows.text: One outcome, such as one word.
a random letter from A to H
The unit when we use ln. One bit is 0.693 nats.

objects.text: Bits = nats / 0.693. Session 16's cross-entropy of 0.299 nats is 0.431 bits.

slides.notes:
The surprise of an outcome x is minus the log of its probability. With log base two the unit is the bit. With the natural logarithm the unit is the nat. For an eighth, minus log two of one eighth is three bits, and minus the natural log is 2.079 nats.

The two differ by the constant factor 0.693, which is ln 2. Libraries use the natural log, so their losses are in nats. Session 16 gave a cross-entropy of 0.299 nats, which is 0.431 bits. Today the hand examples are in bits and the softmax, the loss and the language model are in nats, and every number says which.

title.text:
Entropy is the average surprise, and it is
largest when every outcome is equally likely

objects.alt: Entropy is the average surprise, and it is largest when every outcome is equally likely

objects.text: Entropy H(P) is the average surprise of outcomes drawn from the distribution P.

runs.text: Among two-outcome distributions the fair coin is hardest to predict: 1 bit. The 0.9 coin has only 0.469 bits.
With K equally likely outcomes the entropy is log2 K: 2 bits for 4 words. Our uneven four words have 1.75 bits.

slides.notes:
Entropy is the average surprise. On the left a fair coin, where each outcome has probability one half, so the average surprise is one bit. In the middle a coin that gives heads nine times in ten. Heads is not surprising and tails is very surprising but rare, so the average is only 0.469 bits.

Among all coins, the fair one is hardest to predict. On the right are four next words with entropy 1.75 bits. Four outcomes can hold more uncertainty than two: four equally likely words would give two bits, the most possible for four outcomes. The more outcomes and the more even they are, the higher the entropy.

title.text:
By hand: the entropy of four next words
is the sum of p times surprise, 1.75 bits

objects.text: Illustrative (made-up) probabilities. The total of the last column is the entropy.

slides.notes:
Work it by hand. The first word has probability one half, surprise one bit, and contributes a half. The second has a quarter, two bits, and contributes another half. The last two each have an eighth, three bits, and contribute three eighths each. Add the last column: 0.5, plus 0.5, plus 0.375, plus 0.375 gives 1.75 bits.

These probabilities are made up to give clean arithmetic. If all four words had probability one quarter, each term would be a half and the entropy two bits.

title.text:
Entropy is the probability-weighted
average of the surprise

objects.alt: Entropy is the probability-weighted average of the surprise

rows.text: A distribution: probabilities that add to 1.
Add the terms for every outcome.
The entropy, in bits when the log is base 2.

objects.text: Four equally likely words would have the largest entropy: 2 bits.

slides.notes:
The formula is the table you just filled. Entropy of P is minus the sum over outcomes of p times log two of p. Each term is the probability times its surprise, so entropy is the expectation of the surprise, in the sense of Session 13. For our four words the terms are 0.5, 0.5, 0.375 and 0.375, which add to 1.75 bits.

Entropy depends only on the distribution P. No model is involved, so it is a property of the data. Read the symbol table and say what each symbol means for our four words.

title.text:
Cross-entropy is the average surprise when
reality follows P but the model believes Q

objects.alt: Cross-entropy is the average surprise when reality follows P but the model believes Q

objects.text: Cross-entropy H(P, Q) averages the model's surprise over what really happens.

runs.text: Model A: H(P, Q) = 2.000 bits.
Model B: H(P, Q) = 1.801 bits. Smaller, because Q is closer to P.

slides.notes:
Suppose reality is the distribution on the left, but the model believes one of the other two. Model A spreads probability equally. Model B is closer to reality. Cross-entropy asks how surprised the model is, on average, by what really happens. Each outcome occurs with its true probability, but the model measures the surprise with its own probability.

Model A scores 2.000 bits and Model B scores 1.801. The model that is closer to reality is less surprised, and this number is what training minimises.

title.text:
Cross-entropy weights the model's
surprise by the true probabilities

objects.alt: Cross-entropy weights the model's surprise by the true probabilities

rows.text: The true probability of outcome i.
The probability the model gives to outcome i.
The model's surprise at outcome i is minus this.

objects.text: With a real label, p is 1 on the true class and 0 elsewhere, so the loss is -log q of the true class.

slides.notes:
Cross-entropy is minus the sum of the true probability times the log of the model probability. For model A every q is a quarter, so every surprise is two bits, and the average is exactly two. For model B the number is 1.801. The link to Session 16 comes when we train on a real example.

The true distribution puts probability one on the correct class and zero on the rest. Then the sum has one term, and the loss is minus the log of the probability the model gave to the correct class, the cross-entropy loss you met last time.

title.text:
Cross-entropy is entropy plus KL divergence: the
entropy is fixed, the KL is what the model can improve

objects.alt: Cross-entropy is entropy plus KL divergence: the entropy is fixed, the KL is what the model can improve

slides.notes:
Every bar starts with the entropy of reality, 1.75 bits, in pale grey. No model can go below it, because that is the uncertainty in the data itself. On top of that the model pays a penalty in red, the KL divergence. Model A pays 0.250 bits and Model B only 0.051.

So cross-entropy equals entropy plus KL. During training the entropy of the data does not change, so lowering the cross-entropy is the same as lowering the KL divergence, pulling the model closer to reality. Why can the red part never be negative?

title.text:
KL divergence is never negative and is
zero only when the model equals reality

objects.alt: KL divergence is never negative and is zero only when the model equals reality

rows.text: The extra cost of believing Q when reality is P.
It is 0 only when Q = P everywhere.
D(P || Q) is usually not D(Q || P).
so it is not a distance

objects.text: Minimising cross-entropy over the model is the same as minimising KL, because H(P) is fixed.

slides.notes:
KL divergence is the sum of p times the log of p over q. It measures the extra cost of using the wrong distribution. Three facts. It is never negative. It is zero only when the model equals reality. It is not symmetric, so swapping P and Q gives a different number, which is why we do not call it a distance.

The second line is the link from the picture. Because the entropy is fixed by the data, minimising the cross-entropy over the model minimises the KL. During training you print the cross-entropy, since the entropy of real text is unknown.

title.text:
Recall from Session 12: the softmax turns logits into
probabilities, and the stable form subtracts the largest logit

objects.alt: Recall from Session 12: the softmax turns logits into probabilities, and the stable form subtracts the largest logit

objects.text: Illustrative logits. Stable form (Session 12): subtract the largest logit first. Same p.

slides.notes:
You met the softmax in Session 12, so this is a recall. A model produces one raw score per class, called a logit: 2.0 for cat, 1.0 for dog and 0.1 for fox. The softmax takes the exponential of each, 7.389, 2.718 and 1.105, and divides by their sum, 11.213.

The probabilities are 0.659, 0.242 and 0.099. Session 12 also gave the stable form: subtract the largest logit before the exponential, so that logits like a thousand cannot overflow. The answer does not change. Today adds three things to it: temperature, top-p and its gradient.

title.text:
Temperature divides the logits before the
softmax: a low T sharpens, a high T flattens

objects.alt: Temperature divides the logits before the softmax: a low T sharpens, a high T flattens

objects.text: Each panel adds to 1. T near 0: the top class takes all (greedy). Large T: equal shares.

slides.notes:
In Session 14 you drew a next word by cutting the line from 0 to 1 into slices, one per word, sized by its probability. Temperature changes the slices before the draw. Divide every logit by T, then take the softmax. With T equal to 0.5 the logits double, and cat grows from 0.659 to 0.864.

With T equal to 2 they halve, and cat falls to 0.502 while fox rises. So a low temperature makes the model more predictable and a high temperature spreads the choice. As T goes towards zero the top class takes everything, which is called greedy decoding.

title.text:
Softmax with temperature: one
division, then the same softmax

objects.alt: Softmax with temperature: one division, then the same softmax

rows.text: The temperature, above 0. T = 1 is the plain softmax.
The probability of class i at temperature T.
All classes, the same T in every term.

objects.text: Use the stable form of Session 12 here too: subtract the largest z_j / T first.

slides.notes:
Divide each logit by the temperature T, take e to that power, and divide by the sum over all classes. Work the cat at T equal to two. The logits become 1, 0.5 and 0.05. e to the 1 is 2.718, and the three terms add up to 5.418.

So cat gets 2.718 over 5.418, which is 0.502. The sum must use the same T in every term, otherwise the probabilities will not add to one. With T equal to one you are back at the plain softmax.

title.text:
Top-p (nucleus) sampling keeps the smallest
set of likely words, then rescales them

objects.alt: Top-p (nucleus) sampling keeps the smallest set of likely words, then rescales them

objects.text: Top-p = 0.8: keep the most likely words until their running total reaches 0.8, then rescale them.

runs.text: Tea, coffee and water reach 0.893. Milk and soup are cut. The draw of Session 14 then uses only the kept slices.
Divide by 0.893: tea 0.499, coffee 0.335, water 0.166.

slides.notes:
Top-p sampling, also called nucleus sampling, was published by Holtzman and colleagues in 2020. It removes the thin slices of Session 14 before the draw. These five drinks have illustrative logits, already sorted. With p equal to 0.8, tea gives 0.446, coffee brings the running total to 0.745, and water brings it to 0.893, past 0.8, so we stop.

Milk and soup are cut. The kept probabilities are divided by 0.893 so they add to one again: tea 0.499, coffee 0.335, water 0.166. The next word is drawn at random from those three only.

title.text:
Cross-entropy straight from the logits:
log-softmax is log-sum-exp minus the true logit

objects.alt: Cross-entropy straight from the logits: log-softmax is log-sum-exp minus the true logit

rows.text: The cross-entropy loss for one example, in nats.

objects.text: Session 12 promised this link: libraries compute the loss this way, so no tiny probability is ever formed and logged.

slides.notes:
Training does not compute the probability and then its log. It goes straight from the logits. Take the log of the softmax: the log of e to the z k over the sum is z k minus the log of the sum. That log of a sum of exponentials is the log-sum-exp of Session 12.

For our logits the sum is 11.213 and its log is 2.417. Dog is the true word with logit one, so the loss is 2.417 minus one, 1.417 nats. In bits that would be 2.044. Libraries use this form, with the largest logit subtracted, so a tiny probability is never formed and then logged.

title.text:
Softmax with cross-entropy has a simple gradient
with respect to the logits: prediction minus target

objects.alt: Softmax with cross-entropy has a simple gradient with respect to the logits: prediction minus target

objects.text: Illustrative. Dog, the true word, has a negative gradient: its logit should go up.

slides.notes:
Training needs the gradient of the loss with respect to the logits, and for softmax with cross-entropy it is the prediction minus the target. Dog is the true word, but the model gave it only 0.242. The gradient for dog is -0.758, negative, which tells the optimiser to raise that logit.

The other two entries are positive, 0.659 for cat and 0.099 for fox, so those logits should go down, in proportion to how much probability they took. The three entries add up to zero. The next two slides derive it.

title.text:
Derivation: the gradient of softmax
with cross-entropy is p minus y

objects.alt: Derivation: the gradient of softmax with cross-entropy is p minus y

rows.text: The loss: L = -sum of y_k ln p_k.
1 when k = j, else 0. Not the error signal of backpropagation.
The one-hot target: 1 for the true class.

objects.text: The 1 / p_k cancels p_k. The delta part gives y_j. The other part gives p_j, because the y_k add to 1.

slides.notes:
The loss is minus the sum of y k times the log of p k. First we need how each probability moves when a logit moves: p k times delta k j minus p j. Delta k j is one when k equals j and zero otherwise. It shares a letter with the error signal of Session 11, but here it is only a switch.

The slope of the loss with respect to p k is minus y k over p k. The chain rule with a sum over paths, from Session 9, multiplies and adds them. The p k cancels. Split the sum. The delta part gives y j. The other part gives p j times the sum of the y k, and the y k add up to one. The result is p j minus y j.

title.text:
By hand: how cat and dog move
when the cat logit rises by 0.001

objects.text: The middle slope of the derivation, p_k(delta_kj - p_j), with numbers. Softmax p = (0.659, 0.242, 0.099). Move only the cat logit, z1.
Same class
dp1/dz1 = p1(1 - p1) = 0.659 × 0.341 = 0.225. The quotient rule of Session 7 gives this.
Other class
Check
Recompute the softmax with z1 = 2.001: p1 rises by 0.000225 and p2 falls by 0.000160. Divide by 0.001: 0.225 and -0.160.

slides.notes:
The step that makes or breaks the derivation is how each probability moves when one logit moves. Nudge the cat logit. Cat's own probability moves at the rate p one times one minus p one, 0.659 times 0.341, which is 0.225. You can get that from the quotient rule of Session 7.

Dog's probability moves the other way, at minus p two times p one, -0.160, because the probabilities must still add to one. Now check it. Recompute the softmax with the cat logit at 2.001. Cat rises by 0.000225 and dog falls by 0.000160. Divided by one thousandth those match the formula.

title.text:
By hand: logits 2.0, 1.0, 0.1 with
dog true give a loss of 1.417 nats

objects.text: Illustrative three-class example. The numbers match the lab.
Softmax, target
Loss
Gradient
p - y = (0.659, -0.758, 0.099). The three entries add to 0.
Check
Add 0.001 to the cat logit: the loss rises by about 0.659 × 0.001 = 0.00066.

slides.notes: Put numbers in. The softmax gives 0.659, 0.242 and 0.099. The target is dog. The loss is minus the natural log of 0.242, which is 1.417 nats. The gradient is the prediction minus the target: 0.659, -0.758 and 0.099. They add up to zero. A check you can do on any derivation: nudge the cat logit up by one thousandth, and the loss should rise by about the first gradient entry times one thousandth, which is 0.00066. In the lab you do this for every logit and compare.

title.text:
With two classes the softmax is a sigmoid, so sigmoid
with binary cross-entropy also gives p minus y

objects.alt: With two classes the softmax is a sigmoid, so sigmoid with binary cross-entropy also gives p minus y

rows.text: One logit: the score for class 1.

objects.text: Session 18 uses this form in logistic regression and in the output of its small network.

slides.notes:
Divide the top and the bottom of a two-class softmax by e to the z one, and you get one over one plus e to the minus z one minus z two, which is the sigmoid of Session 11. So a sigmoid is a two-class softmax. Directly: the slope of binary cross-entropy with respect to p is minus y over p plus one minus y over one minus p.

Multiply by the sigmoid slope, p times one minus p. The terms cancel to p minus y. With z equal to 0.5 and y equal to one, p is 0.622 and the gradient is -0.378. Session 18 relies on this form.

title.text:
Perplexity: e raised to the power of the mean
negative log-probability of the real words

objects.alt: Perplexity: e raised to the power of the mean negative log-probability of the real words

objects.text: Mean -ln p = 9.90 / 6 = 1.651 nats. Perplexity = e^1.651 = 5.21.

slides.notes:
A toy language model scores a six word sentence. For each real word, the model had given it a probability, 0.2, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.4 and 0.05. These are made up to show the arithmetic. The red row is minus the natural log of each, and the total is 9.90 nats.

That is the negative log-likelihood of the sentence. Divide by six and the mean is 1.651, the cross-entropy per word in nats. Perplexity is e to that power, 5.21. The weakest words are cat and mat, which got only 0.1 and 0.05, so they add the most to the total.

title.text:
Perplexity is the exponential
of the cross-entropy per token

objects.alt: Perplexity is the exponential of the cross-entropy per token

rows.text: The probability the model gave to the real word i, given the words before it.
The cross-entropy per word, in nats.
Perplexity. In bits it is 2 to the power of the bits per word. Same value.

objects.text: Lower is better. Perplexity 1 means the model gave probability 1 to every real word.

slides.notes:
Perplexity is the exponential of the average negative log-probability of the real words, where each probability is conditional on the words before it, as in Session 15. For our sentence the average is 1.651 nats and the perplexity is 5.21. If you work in bits you take two to the power of the bits per word, and you get the same number, because the unit and the base match.

A perplexity of one means the model gave probability one to every real word. Higher is worse. Read the symbol table and say what N is for our sentence.

title.text:
Perplexity reads as the effective number of
equally likely words the model chooses between

objects.alt: Perplexity reads as the effective number of equally likely words the model chooses between

objects.text: A perplexity of 5.21 means the model is as unsure as if it picked among about five equally likely words.

runs.text: Illustrative numbers.
Compare perplexities only for the same test text and the same tokens.

slides.notes:
Perplexity is the effective number of equally likely choices the model has at each step. A perfect model has perplexity one. A model that guesses uniformly among fifty words has perplexity fifty. Our toy model has 5.21, about five equally likely words per step. One caution. Perplexity depends on how the text is cut into tokens, so only compare models on the same test text and the same tokens.

Whether five is good depends entirely on the text and the tokens.

title.text:
Three common mistakes
about information measures

objects.text: The mistake

runs.text: Cross-entropy and KL divergence are the same thing.
Bits and nats give different perplexities.
A higher temperature makes the model smarter.

objects.text: The fix

runs.text: They differ by the entropy of the data.
Same value if the exponent matches the log base.
It only flattens the probabilities.

objects.text: Always say which log base, which text and which sampling settings.

slides.notes:
Three mistakes. First, cross-entropy and KL are not the same. They differ by the entropy of the data, which training cannot change, so they have the same minimiser but different values. Second, bits and nats do not change the perplexity, as long as you exponentiate with the matching base.

Two to the bits equals e to the nats. Third, a higher temperature does not make a model cleverer. It only flattens the probabilities, so rarer words are drawn more often, which can read as varied or as wrong. Which of the three would you have made?

title.text:
Read the recipe before you write it: entropy,
KL, temperature, top-p, gradient, perplexity

runs.text: H = -np.sum(P * np.log2(P))
kl = np.sum(P * np.log2(P / Q))
p = softmax(z / T)
keep = np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(p5), 0.8) + 1
grad = p - y
ppl = np.exp(np.mean(-np.log(token_probs)))

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: Line 1: entropy in bits.
Line 2: KL divergence. Cross-entropy = H + kl.
Line 3: softmax with temperature T.
Line 4: how many words top-p keeps.
Line 5: the gradient for the logits.
Line 6: perplexity.
Spreadsheet: LOG(q, 2), SUMPRODUCT, a growing SUM, EXP.

slides.notes:
Read the recipe before the lab. Entropy is minus the sum of P times log two of P. KL divergence is the sum of P times log two of P over Q, and cross-entropy is entropy plus that. The softmax with temperature divides the logits by T and then uses the stable softmax.

For top-p, cumsum gives the running total of the sorted probabilities, and searchsorted finds where it first reaches 0.8. The gradient is the prediction minus the target, and perplexity is the exponential of the mean negative log-probability. In a spreadsheet a running total is a SUM whose range grows by one row each time.

The lab has seven steps. In the first you compute the surprise of three events in bits. In the second the entropy of a fair coin, a biased coin and four words. In the third the cross-entropy and the KL divergence of two models, and you confirm that cross-entropy equals entropy plus KL.

In the fourth you rebuild the stable softmax of Session 12. In the fifth you apply a temperature and a top-p cut. In the sixth you check the gradient p minus y against a numeric gradient. In the seventh you compute a perplexity. The spreadsheet has the same numbers on four sheets. Do not skip the predict cells.

Four errors you may meet. A nan from the softmax means the exponential overflowed, so subtract the largest logit first. A message saying not yet, write your code, means a gold cell still holds the placeholder. A negative KL divergence is impossible, so check that P and Q both add to one and that you kept P first.

In the spreadsheet, a divide by zero or a number error means a probability of zero is inside a logarithm. Read the last line of any error first. It usually tells you what to do.

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: pre-training by
minimising cross-entropy on the next token

objects.alt: Where this appears in AI: pre-training by minimising cross-entropy on the next token

objects.text: Published research: transformer language models are pre-trained by minimising next-token cross-entropy.

runs.text: The p - y gradient from today is the signal that starts backpropagation.
Later stages, such as learning from human feedback, use other objectives. Closed products do not publish their internals.

slides.notes:
Published research describes how transformer language models are pre-trained. Text becomes tokens. The network produces one score, a logit, for every word in its vocabulary. A softmax turns the scores into probabilities. During training, the cross-entropy against the real next word is the loss, computed from the logits with log-softmax, and its gradient with respect to the logits is the prediction minus the target, as you derived.

That signal then flows backwards through the network. The exact designs of ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude are not published, so I describe the published framework and make no claim about their internals.

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: temperature
and top-p are settings in public APIs

objects.alt: Where this appears in AI: temperature and top-p are settings in public APIs

objects.text: The next word is drawn at random, so answers can differ. Temperature and top-p set how much.

runs.text: Low temperature: steadier answers. High: more varied.
Nucleus sampling: Holtzman and colleagues, 2020.
Products may add steps we cannot see.

slides.notes:
The public APIs of OpenAI, Google Gemini and Anthropic all document a temperature setting and a top-p setting, and some providers document top-k as well. In the standard definition, temperature divides the logits before the softmax, as you computed. The next word is then drawn at random, so at any temperature above zero the same question can give different answers.

Temperature and top-p set how much they can differ. I am describing the published mathematics. What a product does beyond these settings is not public, so I make no claim about it. Perplexity is also a standard way that published papers report how well a model predicts held-out text.

objects.text: Session 18 teaches attention, the core of a transformer, from parts you have.

runs.text: Each token scores every other token, turns the scores into weights with a softmax, and takes a weighted average.
The new part is how the pieces fit together. You build it by hand.

slides.notes:
A preview of next time. Attention is the core step of a transformer, and Session 18 teaches it as a new idea. Every piece is already yours. A dot product from Session 2 says how well two tokens match. Dividing by the spread of those scores, as in Sessions 13 and 14, keeps them a sensible size.

The softmax of Session 12 and today turns the scores into weights that add to one. And a matrix product from Session 3 takes the weighted average. What is new is how the pieces fit together, and you will build it by hand.

title.text:
Exit check: three questions
and their short answers

rows.text: What is the entropy of a fair coin, in bits?
What is the gradient of softmax with cross-entropy with respect to the logits?
The prediction minus the target: p - y. The same holds for a sigmoid with binary cross-entropy.
A model has a mean negative log-probability of 2.0 nats per word. What is its perplexity?

objects.text: Answer each in one sentence before you read the right-hand column.

slides.notes:
Three questions to finish. One, the entropy of a fair coin is one bit. Two, the gradient of softmax with cross-entropy with respect to the logits is the prediction minus the target, and the sigmoid with binary cross-entropy gives the same form. Three, if the mean negative log-probability is two nats per word, the perplexity is e squared, which is 7.39.

Cover the right-hand column and answer aloud first. If one was shaky, mark it. Next session is the course project, and these three ideas come back there.
